answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth. Most stayed at Carfax (the old chapel); 21 were removed by 1 October, 9 were carried to a Piccadilly house, and 8 of those were found there. Twelve more were found and destroyed at Bermondsey and Mile End. The last box went by ship from London via Varna to Galatz, where it was received by the Count's agent.

First mentioned 26 July 1893 in Mina's journal: Lucy has 'lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep', and Mina has been asked to lock their door at night. Mrs. Westenra raised it with Mina.

Only one: Lucy's diary entry of 12 September 1893 (the garlic-wreath night) never mentions Arthur. Her other entries, the May letters, the August letters and diaries, and the 17 September memorandum all mention him by name.

Four transfusions, in order: Arthur Holmwood (7 Sept, Van Helsing operating, Seward and Van Helsing having planned for Seward to donate); Dr. Seward (10 Sept, with Van Helsing morphia); Van Helsing (13 Sept, Seward operating); Quincey Morris (about 18 Sept, a fourth donor, which Morris himself confirms: 'the blood of four strong men').

The garlic came from Haarlem, from Van Helsing's friend Vanderpool, who grew it in his glass-houses; Van Helsing telegraphed for it. Van Helsing arranged it himself: he placed the flowers in Lucy's room, made the wreath she wore, and fixed garlic at the window and door sashes. Later a boxful arrived each day from Haarlem.

The word 'vampire' first appears on 5 May 1893, in Jonathan Harker's journal, where he notes that the Slovak and Servian peasants speak of something that is 'either were-wolf or vampire' and that he means to ask the Count about the superstitions.

Only one document in the store is in Quincey Morris's own hand: his letter of 25 May 1893 to Arthur Holmwood ('My dear Art'), inviting him to a camp-fire with Jack Seward and signed 'QUINCEY P. MORRIS'. Everything else from him is quoted in other people's diaries and letters.

experience: The task question plus a passage search gave me a usable first hit most of the time, and the grep output with its per-passage ids and dates let me jump straight to read. The `list --source` and `grep --by-entry` views were the most useful: they gave an entry-level count and a title (e.g. 'Letter, Lucy Westenra to Mina Murray'), which made the Lucy and Quincey questions a matter of enumeration rather than guessing. The search ranking was only checked once or twice: on the earth-boxes question the top hits mixed the right passages (the Whitby consignment and the boxes at King's Cross) with a Mina passage on the Professor's plans and a Harker passage on the smell at Carfax, and I did not use search for the other questions because grep gave exact counts. For the vampire question, grep returned passages in date order, but it did not sort them, so I used `grep --before` to confirm the earliest one. Grep also over-matches: my pattern 'Art' pulled in 'heart' and 'start', so I had to go to passage-level reads to check whether Lucy's entries named Arthur. The truncated listing (`... 11 more not shown`) meant I had to rerun with a bigger --limit to see the full set. I wished the tool had told me, for each passage, whether it is the earliest or the last in a sequence, and had a whole-entry text search so I did not need to read every passage. For the transfusions, the donor is often given only in a later passage, so a reader needs to follow the passage that names it; a summary of where each named term first appears would have saved several reads.
